rules.statement: An id with an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate is refused where it enters CoSec, so two different ids never share a stored key: a Redis key is UTF-8, which writes the surrogate as `?`, and tenant `beta\uD800` would read the documents, memberships and revocations of tenant `beta?`. A token that claims one in its subject, tenant, jti, roles or policies is invalid (401 token-invalid) before any revocation is read, and CoSec's token issuer refuses to sign one; a forwarded identity naming one is malformed (400); a control request holding one in its path, query or body is 400; an authenticator, an API key record or a membership provider that gives one has failed (503); cosec-migrate rejects a converted document that holds one (INVALID_ID), and publishes nothing. A surrogate pair is a character like any other. A rate limit key value with one counts in an escaped bucket of its own, never in another value's.

rules.statement: A token's tenant claim names a tenant or is absent. Absent, the principal is in the default tenant (0). An empty claim makes the token invalid (401 token-invalid) on every path that verifies one, the pipeline's and refresh's, whichever verifier read it: read as no tenant, it would put the principal in the default tenant with the token's roles. A claim that cannot name a tenant document (blank, `*`, holding `:` or a control character, longer than 128 characters: the rule of `SnapshotKey.Tenant`) makes the token invalid as well, and an API key record with such a tenant fails (503), so every credential applies one rule. CoSec's issuer refuses to sign a token with an empty tenant or one it would refuse.

rules.statement: An id beginning with ( is CoSec's, as the tenants (0) and (platform) and the space (default): a token whose subject begins with ( is invalid, on every path that verifies one, and none is issued. Whether a principal is authenticated is stated by the pipeline, never read off its id.

rules.statement: A refresh token (the claim cosec.token, which the converter writes as refresh) is invalid wherever an access token is expected, on every path that verifies one: signed and unexpired, it never authenticates as a principal, so a principal named after the access token's id cannot exist. A token without the claim is an access token, whoever issued it. The other way too: a refresh reads only a refresh token where one belongs, issued with the access token it is presented with (its sub is that token's jti, its iat that token's iat); an access token there is refused, so whoever holds a token of a principal named after another token's id cannot refresh that token.

jwt:JwtTokenVerifierTest#anAccessTokenIsRefusedWhereARefreshTokenIsExpected

rules.statement: A token is never issued from an earlier token on a revocation read that failed: a refresh, or a tenant switch, whose revocations cannot be read (RevocationUnavailableException) fails, never reads the earlier token as not revoked, so a revoked token, or a token of a revoked principal, cannot be refreshed or switched into one that no revocation names. The pipeline's degraded verification (PIP-7) applies to verifying a token only.

rules.statement: Only a family's current generation moves it: a refresh of the current generation moves the family to its next generation with a conditional write of the record it read, so of concurrent refreshes of one pair exactly one moves it, on one instance or many. A refresh of any other generation never moves it.

rules.statement: The generation the family just replaced, presented within cosec.jwt.session.rotation-leeway of the move, is answered with a pair of the current generation and moves nothing: a refresh whose response was lost can be retried, and two tabs refreshing one pair both keep a usable pair. The window opens at the move and does not slide. Any older generation, or the one just replaced after the leeway, revokes the whole family and is refused, so a copied pair, even one answered within the leeway, is caught at the next refresh after it.

rules.statement: A family ends cosec.jwt.session.lifetime after its login, however often it was refreshed: a refresh after that is refused and the user signs in again, no pair outlives that end, and a tenant switch, which does not sign the user in again, keeps the login time.

rules.statement: A logout ends the session: TokenRevoker revokes the family and the access token's id, from the access token while it is valid and from the pair (bound as a refresh requires) once it has expired, so no pair of the family refreshes afterwards, the pairs it was refreshed from included. The family is marked revoked, never deleted, until its end.

rules.statement: A family record that cannot be read, or a write of it that cannot be confirmed, issues nothing: the refresh fails (503), never reads the family as absent or the write as done. A missing record refuses the refresh (401).

rules.statement: A social sign-in's callback is accepted only with a state CoSec issued, once, and only from the browser that started the sign-in: the state is taken from the SocialStateStore (removed atomically) before the provider is called, whatever follows, and the browser's binding must hash to the one recorded with the state. A callback whose state is unknown, expired, already used or issued to another browser is refused, and the provider is never called for it.

rules.statement: A principal's attributes cannot be changed once its authenticator has returned it: they are what the host reads from its SecurityContext and what every further check of the request decides on (subject.attributes.*). AuthenticatedPrincipal keeps a read-only view of the map it is handed, and CoSec's token verifier makes the attributes claim read-only at every level, nested objects and arrays included. A change through the principal, at any level, throws, and a further check decides as the first did; what is read is what the authenticator handed over.

rules.statement: A tenant switch issues only from a live session, and only on its token pair: the switch presents the request's own access token and its refresh token, checked as a refresh's are, and an access token alone, or a pair the request was not made with, issues nothing (401 token-invalid). The session is the request's, as CoSec's token proved it, whose family is readable, its principal's and tenant's, not revoked and not ended, with the token's revocations read strictly (IDN-14), and the pair is one the session would refresh, by the refresh's own rule: the current generation, or the one just replaced within the rotation leeway; an older pair presented to switch is a pair presented again, which revokes the session as a refresh would (IDN-16). The switch moves nothing of the session it was presented from. Otherwise nothing is issued: 401 when the session is unknown, another's, revoked or ended, 503 when the family or the revocations cannot be read (IDN-19). A refresh checks its session in the same place, so a family revoked by a logout (IDN-18) or by a pair presented again (IDN-16) issues nothing, by either.

rules.source: RFC 0009 §11.3; docs/roadmap.md §9 as of commit 8b881ed3 (the starter serves the refresh route)
rules.statement: When cosec.authentication.login.refresh.path is set, the starter serves POST on it, on Spring MVC and on WebFlux, under the pipeline like every route (STA-4: a document must permit an anonymous POST of it; nothing is exempted from the filter), and never on a gateway. Its body is exactly {"accessToken","refreshToken"} as application/json, at most 32 KiB; anything else is 400 invalid-request. It answers 200 application/json, the CompositeToken written by CoSec's one mapper; 401 token-expired, token-revoked or token-invalid for a refusal of the pair; 503 unavailable when the revocations or the session store cannot answer (nothing issued, nothing spent: IDN-14, IDN-19); 500 internal-error for any other error, never 401. Every answer carries Cache-Control: no-store, a problem body is ProblemEncoder's and carries nothing of the request but its request id, and no log line of CoSec carries a token. A path set where the route cannot be served fails startup (STA-1).

rules.statement: When cosec.authentication.login.logout.path is set, the starter serves POST on it as it serves the refresh route (IDN-23): the pair in the body, TokenRevoker.revoke of the pair, whether or not the access token has expired. It answers 204 when the session is ended, and when it already was (token-revoked), so a logout whose answer was lost can be sent again; 401 for a pair that is not one; 503 when the store cannot record it; 500 for any other error; 400 for a body that is not the pair; Cache-Control: no-store on every answer.

rules.statement: A request, a refresh and a logout verify with one TokenVerifier: the application's bean when it declares one, else CoSec's. The served refresh route refreshes with the application's RefreshTokenAuthentication when it declares one, its hook included, else with the starter's over the MembershipRefresh bean; a refresh authentication over a credentials class the route cannot present fails startup while the route's path is set.

rules.statement: A revocation through TokenRevoker invalidates every instance's local 'not revoked' answer for that token or subject at once; an instance that missed the invalidation keeps that answer for at most 30 seconds (RevokedTokenCache.MISSING_TTL_SECONDS), and no property, layer or customizer lengthens it. A revocation an instance holds locally, a subject revocation raised since included, is kept at most as long (DR1-D-3): both tables' local-max-age, as the cache ends with it, is at most 30 seconds: cosec.authentication.revocation.cache.local-max-age, a cocache.* property or a customizer above it fails startup, and a layer may only tighten it.

rules.statement: CoSec's tokens are signed: JwtTokenVerifier and JwtTokenConverter refuse Algorithm.none() when they are built, so no unsigned token is issued, and none is accepted as CoSec's own (and so eligible for break-glass, BRK-8).

rules.statement: CoSec's token verifier tolerates an issuer's clock ahead of its own by the skew (`cosec.authentication.revocation.skew`, the one subject revocation judges with): a token's `iat` and `nbf` may be that much later than the verifier's clock. Never its `exp`: no skew lengthens a token's life. A token beyond the skew is rejected as `TOKEN_NOT_YET_VALID`, which the client reads as `token-invalid`.

rules.statement: A token never passes for another kind of credential: a verified token whose `attributes` hold one CoSec sets for another credential (`apiKeyId`, which names the API key a request was authenticated with) is rejected as `TOKEN_INVALID`, so an ALLOW written for one key never permits a token that claims to be it, and `JwtTokenConverter` issues no such token.

rules.statement: A session record (a token family) carries its format and is read by the reader's rule: a member a later version adds is ignored, a record written before formats is format 1, and a later format is refused, which ends that session, never reads as another one.

rules.source: Review round 2, R2B-22: the cache of verified tokens; RFC 0009 §11.5
rules.statement: A cached verification is what verifying the token again would answer: CoSec's verifier answers from its cache only while its own clock is where verifying again would succeed, so a cached token never outlives its `exp` nor precedes its `iat` and `nbf` beyond the skew, and a token that differs in any byte is verified again; only successes are kept, and the revocation and reserved-attribute checks run after it on every request. The cache holds the token cache's share of the heap (`STA-12`), each entry weighed by its token's length times what an entry measurably retains for a character; the weight is reckoned when an entry is put, on a miss, never on a hit, and an evicted entry costs one verification, never another answer. Refresh, tenant switch and logout never read it, and an application's own TokenVerifier is never given it.

rules.source: Coordinator's brief for 8.0.0-beta.6, 2026-11-21 (the properties review, items 22, 23 and 26; memory by heap share); RFC 0006 §9.3
rules.statement: Each revocation table's local copy (`RevokedTokenCache`, `RevokedSubjectCache`) holds the revocation tables' share of the heap (`STA-12`), counted in entries of their measured size (290 and 230 bytes): the starter declares the count, and CoSec locks it, so neither `cocache.defaults.store.*` nor a customizer changes it, and a `cocache.caches.[name]` property that sets it fails startup. A smaller copy only sends more revocation reads to Redis; it never answers "not revoked" for longer.

rules.source: Roadmap §4 (beta.5: a service caller first declared api-key, a method of its own before RC1); coordinator's decision of 2026-11-23 (design (b): AuthenticatedPrincipal.workload); RFC 0009 §3, §4.2, RFC 0010 C3 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: The identity a service states for itself when it calls the control plane as its own principal (ControlCaller.service, ServiceIdentity), in process or over the network, names its credential `service`, never `api-key` or `jwt`, with the id `service:<principal>`, and audit and decision records name the method so. A change record's origin names how the call came (CTL-57): `via.method: service` over the network, and `via.method: in-process` through the in-process facade (CTL-65), each with the credential id `service:<principal>`. `service` and `api-key` are CoSec's workload methods: a principal is a workload's (AuthenticatedPrincipal.workload) when CoSec's API key authenticator proved it (by provenance) or its credential is named `api-key` or `service`, whoever named it: a gateway's forwarded identity, a service's stated one, or another authenticator's (fail closed). What a principal may do as a person or as a workload is read from workload alone, never from apiKey, which keeps its meaning (an API key proved it): a workload never approves (APR-7) and is never the trust root (APR-3). A `service` credential, as any credential but CoSec's own token, has no session and no break-glass. A principal any other authenticator proves is a person unless its credential names `api-key` or `service`: an authenticator of machine clients names its credentials `Identity.Method.SERVICE` (or `API_KEY`) to make them workloads, and one that names another method is trusted to prove people (an S3 of the RC1 review, DR1-C-3; a person by provenance only is 8.1's).

rules.source: RC1 deep review DR1-G-2 (round-1-g-host.md); the coordinator's ruling of 2026-11-23; RFC 0009 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: A session record (a token family) is kept from each write for the shorter of what is left of its lifetime and the refresh token validity (cosec.jwt.token-validity.refresh), so a session nobody refreshes leaves the store with its last refresh token; and a store keeps, for each principal in each tenant, the TokenFamilyStore.SESSIONS_PER_PRINCIPAL (64) sessions that began most recently: creating one more deletes the record of the one that began earliest, live, revoked or ended, whose next refresh is then refused as an unknown session. CoSec's stores count a session before they write its record, so none escapes the count.

rules.source: RC1 deep review, the coordinator's third batch, 2026-11-23; RFC 0004 §4.5.3, RFC 0009 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: A token revocation is kept past the end of every token it can name, so no revoked token is valid again when its record expires: the starter keeps a token's or a subject's revocation for the longer of cosec.jwt.token-validity.access and cosec.jwt.token-validity.refresh, plus cosec.authentication.revocation.skew (an issuer's clock may run that far ahead, IDN-29), computed and never configured, and the control plane's check that a revocation outlives an approval reads the same value. No token outlives that retention: CoSec's issuer refuses a call that asks for an access or refresh validity longer than the configured one, naming the property.

rules.source: RC1 deep review, the coordinator's third batch and ruling of 2026-11-23; RFC 0009 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: A session a tenant switch starts names its root, the session its user's login began (the switched session's root, or that session when it is the login's own), and lives only while the root does: its refresh, the retry within the rotation leeway, and a switch from it each read the root, and a root ended, revoked or gone revokes it and refuses (401 token-revoked). Each such answer writes the root back unchanged with a conditional write, so the root is kept as long as a session that depends on it, and a switch back to the root's tenant begins the root again in its principal's count (IDN-35). A switch reads back the session it created and is refused, ending it, when the store did not keep the root. Such a record is written as format 2, which a reader of format 1 refuses (IDN-31).

rules.source: #1889 (RFC 0004 §4.1); the coordinator's review of 2026-11-23 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: A principal id is not blank: neither empty nor white space only. Authenticated means someone, and the id keys the principal's sessions, revocations, rate limits and audit records. Each entrance refuses one in its own terms: a token whose subject is blank is invalid (401 token-invalid) on every path that verifies one, a request's and a refresh's, and CoSec's token issuer signs none; a forwarded identity whose sub, tenant or rid is blank is malformed (400), and a gateway writes none; an API key record of a blank principal cannot be made, so its lookup fails (503); a document binding a blank principal, a stored actor or a session record naming one does not decode; cosec-migrate names a 7.x API key of a blank principal among its rejections and converts the others. PrincipalId itself refuses a blank value, so an authenticator of the application's own that makes one has failed (503), as for IDN-10. An id is not trimmed: white space around one is part of it, compared as it is.

rules.source: DR2-F-1, DR2-C-1 (the coordinator's ruling and the maintainer's word to add the member, 2026-11-23); RFC 0006 §7, RFC 0007 §10.2 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: The CoSec-Identity header states the principal's whole memberships: beside `roles` (the roles of the decided space), `memberships` holds its roles in every other space (`spaces`, by space id, the default space's key empty) and the ids of the policies it attaches (`attachments`, in the order its memberships name them). CoSec's writers, the gateway's forward and HttpControlService's relay of a request's caller, always write it, empty when there is nothing more; a service identity states it empty. The decided space is never a key of `spaces`, nor `*`; a space names at least one role; a role or an attachment is a non-empty id with no unpaired surrogate, never repeated. A host that decides with policies on the identity (cosec.pipeline.caller=forwarded-identity: a control host, a service port) refuses a header without `memberships` as malformed (400 invalid-request), and builds the caller's memberships from `roles` under the decided space, `memberships.spaces` and `memberships.attachments`, so a DENY attached to the principal, or one that reads a role it holds in another space, applies there as at the gateway and in process; a service that only trusts the gateway does not require it. An identity too large for the header with them is not forwarded: the gateway fails the request (500) and the relay fails the call before it is sent, never cut short.

rules.source: The maintainer's answer of 2026-11-24 (a logout after a tenant switch ends the login it came from too); RFC 0009 §11.4 (sentences proposed in the PR)
rules.statement: Logging out of a session a tenant switch started ends the login it was switched from (its root, IDN-36) as well, through every logout of CoSec's revoker: TokenRevoker.revoke of the access token, of the pair, and the served logout route (IDN-24); the root is read from the session's record, so the access token alone suffices. The root is revoked first, then the session, then the token's id, each by a conditional write, so a refresh or a switch that read the root before cannot write it back live, and a logout that fails at a step has done none of the later ones: it is answered as a failure (503 when the store cannot read or write), never as done while the login lives on, and its retry starts again. A root already revoked or gone is left as it is, a root of another principal is left alone and logged, and a login's own logout ends only itself. A switched session whose record is gone (pushed out of its principal's latest sessions in its tenant, IDN-35) cannot find its root. The access tokens the root and the other sessions switched from it issued stay valid until they expire, and those sessions end at their next refresh or switch.
